title: The project manager
blurb: What the project manager is responsible for day to day, what they own, and exactly when they must escalate.
question: A library refurbishment is running a week late because a contractor's crew was off sick. The end date can still be met by re-ordering some work. Should the project manager deal with this personally, or take it to the sponsor?

teach.h: The person who makes it happen
teach.body: APM describes the project manager as responsible for the day-to-day management of the project: planning, organising, leading the team, monitoring and controlling, so that the outputs are delivered to the agreed time, cost, quality and scope. In plain English: the sponsor decides what the organisation needs and why; the project manager works out how to deliver it and then runs the work until the outputs are handed over.

teach.centre:
Deliver to
time, cost,
quality, scope
teach.caption: This loop repeats throughout deployment: compare progress with the plan, correct course, and report to the sponsor.

teach.body: The sponsor delegates authority to the project manager within tolerances: agreed limits of permitted deviation on things like time and cost. Inside those limits the project manager decides and acts, then reports. When a tolerance is threatened, the project manager warns the sponsor early. When a problem breaches, or is about to breach, a tolerance it becomes an issue, and the project manager escalates it so the sponsor can agree a resolution.

teach.h: How far can the project manager go?

bands.label: Within tolerance: PM decides and reports
Tolerance threatened: warn the sponsor early
Tolerance breached: an issue for the sponsor

teach.caption: Example only: a sponsor might allow ±2 weeks on time and ±£20,000 on cost. The figures are agreed per project.

teach.body: Sam is project manager; the council's Head of Culture is sponsor. Sam wrote the project management plan, which the sponsor approved. Sam's time tolerance is two weeks. When a contractor loses a week to sickness, Sam re-sequences decorating and shelving, keeps the end date, logs the change and reports it. Later, asbestos is found and Sam forecasts a five-week delay: beyond tolerance, so Sam escalates it as an issue with options for the sponsor to decide.

teach.text: Classic distractors for the project manager: 'chairs the steering group', 'owns the business case', 'approves the funding', 'accountable for benefits'. Those are all the sponsor. The project manager is RESPONSIBLE for delivering the outputs; the sponsor is ACCOUNTABLE for the project meeting its need and realising the benefits.

items: Project manager: responsible for the day-to-day management of the project.
Plans, organises, leads, monitors and controls to deliver outputs to agreed time, cost, quality and scope.
Writes, owns and maintains the project management plan; the sponsor approves it.
Manages risks and resolves day-to-day problems within tolerance; escalates issues (problems beyond tolerance) to the sponsor and reports progress.

summary: You can now describe the project manager's day-to-day responsibilities, name the documents the project manager owns or contributes to, and explain how delegated tolerances decide what the project manager handles and what goes to the sponsor.

A.q: Which role is responsible for the day-to-day management of a project?
A.why: The project manager is responsible for day-to-day management: planning, organising, leading, monitoring and controlling the work.

whyNot.0: The sponsor is accountable at a senior level and delegates day-to-day management to the project manager.
whyNot.2: The governance board gives direction and makes key decisions; it does not run the project daily.
whyNot.3: The product owner prioritises the backlog and represents users on iterative work; overall day-to-day management is the project manager's.

A.q: Which document does the project manager write, own and maintain?
A.why: The project manager writes, owns and maintains the project management plan; the sponsor approves it.

whyNot.0: The sponsor owns the business case; the project manager contributes to it.
whyNot.1: On iterative work the product owner owns the product backlog.
whyNot.2: Portfolio strategy is set at organisational level, not by a project manager.

A.q: Complete the statement: the project manager manages risks and resolves day-to-day problems within…
A.why: The sponsor delegates authority within tolerances. Inside them the project manager manages risks and resolves problems; a problem beyond them is an issue, which the PM escalates to the sponsor.

whyNot.0: PMO standards shape how things are done but do not set the limits of the PM's authority.
whyNot.2: The business case justifies the project; it does not define the PM's limits of authority.
whyNot.3: The sponsor's availability has nothing to do with the PM's authority to act.

B.q: To whom does the project manager normally report progress?
B.why: The project manager reports progress to the sponsor (and through the sponsor to the governance board).

whyNot.0: End users are kept informed and engaged, but they are not who the project manager reports to.
whyNot.1: The product owner works with the team on priorities; the PM's reporting line is to the sponsor.
whyNot.3: The team reports progress to the project manager, not the other way round.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a project manager responsibility?
B.why: The sponsor owns the business case. The project manager contributes estimates and delivery input to it.

whyNot.1: Leading the team is a core project manager responsibility.
whyNot.2: Monitoring and controlling progress against the plan is day-to-day management.
whyNot.3: The project manager owns and maintains the project management plan.

B.q:
Which TWO statements describe the project manager?
1) Delivers the outputs to agreed time, cost, quality and scope
2) Is accountable for realising the benefits
3) Escalates when tolerances are threatened
4) Chairs the governance board
B.why: The project manager delivers the outputs to the agreed parameters (1) and escalates when tolerances are threatened (3).

whyNot.0: Accountability for benefits (2) belongs to the sponsor.
whyNot.1: Chairing the governance board (4) is usually the sponsor's role.

C.q: Testing on a website project overruns by three days. The time tolerance is two weeks and the end date is still safe. What should the project manager do?
options: Escalate it to the sponsor as an issue
Re-plan within tolerance and report it
Ask the board to approve a new plan
Raise a change to the business case
C.why: The delay is within the project manager's delegated tolerance, so the PM resolves it and keeps the sponsor informed through normal reporting.

whyNot.0: It is not an issue in the APM sense because it does not breach or threaten the tolerance.
whyNot.2: The board does not need to approve action the PM is authorised to take.
whyNot.3: A small delay that leaves the end date intact does not change the project's justification.

C.q: A project manager forecasts finishing six weeks late against a four-week time tolerance. What should happen next?
options: Escalate to the sponsor for a decision
Move the end date in the baseline
Ask the PMO to approve a new date
Drop some scope with the team's agreement
C.why: The forecast breaches the tolerance, so it is an issue. The project manager escalates it, with options, for the sponsor to agree a resolution.

whyNot.1: Changing the baseline end date needs authority beyond the PM's tolerance and goes through change control.
whyNot.2: The PMO supports and reports; it does not hold the sponsor's decision-making authority.
whyNot.3: Cutting agreed scope without the sponsor's approval would bypass governance and change control.

C.q: During definition, the sponsor needs cost and time figures for the business case. How is the project manager involved?
options: Owns and approves the business case
Has no role until deployment starts
Signs off the funding for the project
C.why: The project manager supports the business case with estimates of time, cost and resources and delivery planning; the sponsor owns it.

whyNot.0: Ownership and approval of the business case sit with the sponsor.
whyNot.1: The project manager is usually appointed early enough to contribute to definition.
whyNot.3: Securing and releasing funding is a sponsor responsibility.

reteach.title: The project manager is the wedding planner
reteach.question: A couple hire a wedding planner and give them a budget with a little leeway. Which decisions can the planner make alone, and which must go back to the couple?

blocks.body: The couple (the sponsor) decide what kind of day they want and hold the money. The planner (the project manager) builds the plan, books suppliers, coordinates everyone on the day and keeps the couple updated. If the florist needs £50 more and the leeway covers it, the planner just handles it and mentions it later. If the venue cancels, the planner brings options to the couple, because that decision is theirs.

blocks.text: The planner never decides whether the wedding is still worth having, and the couple never chase the caterer. Same with projects: the PM runs delivery, the sponsor owns the reasons and the big calls.

explain.body: The project manager is responsible for the day-to-day management of the project: planning, organising, leading the team, monitoring and controlling, so outputs are delivered to the agreed time, cost, quality and scope.

items.label: parameters: time, cost, quality and scope

test.q: What best summarises the project manager's role?
options: Managing the project day to day
test.why: The project manager is responsible for the day-to-day management of the project to deliver its outputs.

whyNot.0: Strategy is set at senior and portfolio level, not by the project manager.
whyNot.1: Using the outputs is the role of end users.
whyNot.3: Setting organisation-wide standards is a typical PMO function.

explain.body: The project manager writes, owns and maintains the project management plan: why, what, how, who, when and how much. The sponsor approves it, and the PM keeps it up to date, for example after an approved change.

test.q: After a change request is approved, who updates the project management plan?
test.why: The project manager owns and maintains the project management plan, so updates after an approved change are the PM's job.

whyNot.0: The sponsor approves the plan but does not maintain it.
whyNot.1: A PMO may supply templates or check compliance, but the plan belongs to the PM.
whyNot.2: End users use the outputs; they do not maintain project plans.

explain.body: Tolerances are the limits of deviation the sponsor delegates to the project manager. Inside them the PM manages risks, resolves day-to-day problems and corrects course without asking. A problem beyond them is an issue for the sponsor.

test.q: In project management, what is a tolerance?
options: The float on any non-critical activity
The total budget held by the sponsor
The time a team member may be absent
test.why: A tolerance is the agreed permitted deviation (for example on time or cost) within which the project manager can act without escalating.

whyNot.1: Float is scheduling flexibility on an activity, not delegated authority.
whyNot.2: The sponsor secures the budget, but a tolerance is a permitted deviation, not the budget itself.
whyNot.3: Absence has nothing to do with the limits of the PM's authority.

explain.body: The project manager reports progress to the sponsor regularly, and escalates as soon as a tolerance is threatened, so the sponsor can decide in time rather than being surprised.

test.q: When should a project manager escalate to the sponsor?
options: Only at the final closure review
Only if the team asks them to
test.why: The project manager escalates when delegated tolerances are threatened or breached, giving the sponsor time to decide.

whyNot.0: Waiting until closure would leave the sponsor no chance to act.
whyNot.1: Small slips within tolerance are the PM's to manage; escalating them all would swamp the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Escalation depends on tolerances, not on whether the team requests it.
